items.title: Nonprofit fundraising platforms like GoFundMe Pro, DonorPerfect are under attack ahead of Giving Tuesday: It’s ‘like we were in the Situation Room’
items.summary:
On Nov. 10, DonorPerfect, a fundraising software and CRM platform for nonprofits, made the “ difficult decision ” to go offline as attacks were being attempted on its systems. 

“It was just almost like we were in the Situation Room, and we’re like, ‘just take it down, so that we know that they can’t get through,’” Lauren Sheehan, DonorPerfect’s president, told Fortune .

DonorPerfect has confirmed unauthorized activity involving certain of its systems. The company said it engaged cybersecurity experts to investigate and temporarily restricted access to DonorPerfect and certain related services while it put protective measures in place. 

Sheehan described taking the system down as a preemptive security measure. The company said its investigation included assessing whether customer information was accessed without authorization. 

The shutdown left DonorPerfect’s 11,000 customers without access to the system right before what’s historically the busiest giving season of the year. Nonprofits received 37% of all 2025 online revenue in December, according to M+R’s annual Benchmarks study , and Americans donated a whopping $4 billion on Giving Tuesday last year.

“It’s really difficult to tell your 11,000 customers that their system isn’t available,” she said, adding that many nonprofits raise anywhere from 30% to 50% of their fundraising goals in the last two to three months of the year. 

But customers have largely understood that DonorPerfect’s move was made out of an “abundance of caution,” Sheehan said. “We wanted to take the systems offline until we were totally and…
items.t: Nonprofit fundraising platforms like GoFundMe Pro, DonorPerfect are under attack ahead of Giving Tuesday: It’s ‘like we were in the Situation Room’

items.title: The Jensen Huang problem: Why CEOs who replace founders are more likely to flame out
items.summary:
On its Tuesday earnings call , the first since founder and CEO Jensen Huang resigned, Nvidia’s board confirmed it has hired a search firm to find his successor and that it will consider both internal and external candidates. Whoever gets the job will inherit one of the toughest assignments in corporate America. 

That’s partly because Nvidia, one of the world’s most valuable companies and the engine of the AI boom, faces sky-high expectations, rising competition, and geopolitical headwinds. But it’s also because the new chief will take on one of business’s most notoriously difficult jobs: following a founder. Huang built Nvidia from the ground up, earned fierce loyalty from employees, and came to personify the company itself, leaving behind a shadow that successors will struggle to escape.

“The attitude that somebody has to have when they’re replacing an iconic founder is that ‘there is no way I am going to outshine this person,’ and redirect the focus away from the iconic person,” says Robert Kelley, professor of management at Carnegie Mellon University’s Tepper School of Business. Instead, he adds, the approach of a successor should be “watch what I can do for this business.” 

The first problem for a founder-CEO’s successor is often the founder themselves. A founder has typically dedicated a big chunk of their life to building the firm. A 2024 Spencer Stuart analysis found that founder-CEOs served 21 years on average before their exit, nearly three times as long as the average 7.4-year tenure of S&P 500 CEOs. Even after they leave the CEO job, founders tend to linger…
items.t: The Jensen Huang problem: Why CEOs who replace founders are more likely to flame out

items.title: TJMaxx’s parent company is spending one-third of its $463 million in tariff refunds on corporate bonuses—and it’s not the only one
items.summary:
TJX , the parent of TJ Maxx and Marshalls, has now set aside $167 million of its $463 million in tariff refunds for bonuses and incentive pay, the company disclosed Wednesday —and it plans to keep booking bonus costs next quarter, even though it isn’t expecting any more refunds. The discretionary bonuses are for “non-executive” associates, according to the filing. 

The move follows what U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer told companies to do back in March : pass refunds along to workers as a bonus or a raise, “because that’s the purpose of the program,” he said. 

Giving tariff refunds back to employees raises questions about whether consumers will see refunds reach their wallets. A Federal Reserve Bank of New York analysis found nearly 90% of the tariffs’ economic burden fell on U.S. firms and consumers. TJX hasn’t said it will lower prices.

TJX isn’t alone. As U.S. companies scrape back more than $100 billion in tariff refunds, some are using those rebates for company bonuses rather than passing them back down to customers who bore the brunt of the levies.

Publicly traded companies, including Titleist-maker Acushnet, and industrial tool producer Stanley Black & Decker, have disclosed plans to use millions of dollars returned to dole out to employees, including executives. ProPublica, which first reported the trend this week, identified at least nine public companies doing the same.

While some companies , such as FedEx , have pledged to give the cash from the refunds back to consumers, and companies like Walmart and Target have committed to lowering prices as a…
items.t: TJMaxx’s parent company is spending one-third of its $463 million in tariff refunds on corporate bonuses—and it’s not the only one

items.title: One hand on the controller, one on the pizza roll: How America fed itself through GTA VI’s $3.79 billion launch night
items.summary:
The biggest video game launch in years left millions of players with a practical problem: how to eat without putting down the controller.

Rockstar Games, a unit of Take-Two Interactive, said the game brought in an estimated $3.79 billion in retail sales worldwide on its first day, which it called the biggest entertainment launch in history. With that demand, there are surely some tired people holding onto those controllers but hungry for a snack.

It seems like the delivery apps already planned for it. Uber Eats picked several of its Grand Theft Auto VI launch-day deals for food that could be eaten with one hand. In the U.S., the list included buy-one-get-one McNuggets at McDonald’s, boneless wings at Wingstop, pizza at Papa John’s and Whopper Jr. burgers at Burger King.

“We even picked some of our food deals with one-handed eating in mind, so fans can keep their focus on the game,” Uber President and COO Andrew Macdonald said in a statement to Fortune .

Gamers ordered accordingly. Between midnight and 5 a.m. on launch night, Uber Eats orders in Miami, the real city behind the game’s Vice City, rose more than 30% from the prior two Thursdays, Macdonald said on X . Nationwide, orders of Red Bull Watermelon rose 95%, Totino’s Pizza Rolls 54% and Ghost Sour Strips 46%. Uber told Fortune it had no separate data on one-handed food orders.

DoorDash reported a similar pattern. Between 9 p.m. and 2 a.m. ET, orders for chips, burgers, fries and pizza each rose more than 10% compared with the average of the six prior Wednesdays, the company told Fortune . Energy drinks rose more…

items.title: BNP Paribas sees ‘panic selling’ as the AI selloff drags the S&P 500 into a correction and wipes out the Nasdaq’s 2026 gains
items.summary:
The S&P 500 fell into a correction Friday, and the Nasdaq Composite gave back everything it had gained in 2026.

The S&P 500 closed more than 10% below its Oct. 6 record close, and the Dow also ended in correction territory. The S&P fell 3.59% to 6,918.45, its seventh straight losing session and its longest losing streak since February 2020.

Investors were “panic selling” as they tried to judge whether enthusiasm for AI had peaked, Benedicte Lowe, an equity derivatives strategist at BNP Paribas , told CNBC .

Anthropic led the AI slide, as Fortune reported Friday morning . The Claude maker raised $81.34 billion in an IPO that valued it at $1.414 trillion, and its shares fell about 9% Friday, their second day of trading, giving back much of Thursday’s 17% pop. Reuters cited worries about slower data-center expansion, higher borrowing costs and Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO. Huang resigned on Nov. 12, and CFO Colette Kress is interim CEO.

The people with the most money in stocks already felt it. Those with the largest stockholdings reported a decline in personal finances in the University of Michigan’s November survey, which ran through Nov. 16, “consistent with continued AI-related agitation in stock markets,” survey director Joanne Hsu said .

What the panic looked like 

Chipmakers took the worst of it. Micron , hotlink]Broadcom[/hotlink], Nvidia, and AMD were down between roughly 12% and 14%. The VIX, Wall Street’s fear gauge, topped 30 for the first time since March, CNBC reported.

The selling wasn’t only in the U.S. Taiwan’s stock index fell 5.65% Friday,…
items.t: BNP Paribas sees ‘panic selling’ as the AI selloff drags the S&P 500 into a correction and wipes out the Nasdaq’s 2026 gains

items.title: Fed governor admits people now think higher inflation is the new normal: ‘That’s the kind of psychology we need to start breaking’
items.summary:
Fed Governor Chris Waller says Americans are starting to treat 3% inflation as normal, and he thinks the central bank may need to “shock people” out of it.

The latest consumer price index also showed inflation is heating up more than expected, drifting further away from the Fed’s 2% target. And given that it’s been above that threshold for more than five years, it’s getting harder for consumers and businesses to see higher prices as a temporary blip. 

In a CNBC interview on Wednesday, Waller warned that inflation is spreading beyond the areas most affected by higher energy prices or tariffs, including into so-called core services. He recalled talking to someone last week who said his business passed on a 3% price hike to consumers because that’s what he thinks his customers can swallow.

“And that’s when you start having problems of trying to get inflation down,” Waller explained. “So you might need to, like, shock people to say, ‘Wait a minute, 3% is not the number you should be thinking about going forward.’” 

Once households and businesses expect prices to keep rising 3% a year, they set wages and prices to match, the kind of spiral the Fed worries about after more than five years above its 2% target. 

Maintaining consumers’ inflation expectations is a top priority for the Fed. It previously held off on a more hawkish stance, saying expectations were still well anchored. But in Waller’s view, that’s no longer the case.

“People are starting to think 3% may be the norm. And if you’re a firm, and the consumer’s resilient and seems to be spending, why not pass through…
items.t: Fed governor admits people now think higher inflation is the new normal. ‘That’s the kind of psychology we need to start breaking’

The company behind the popular AI chatbot Claude debuted on the Nasdaq Thursday, initially raising $81.3 billion in a public offering that surpassed the previous record of $75 billion SpaceX’s IPO initially brought in over the summer. On Friday, Anthropic announced that underwriters had purchased millions more shares, bringing the offering’s total to about $93.5 billion.

After pricing its shares at $83 apiece on Wednesday, the company opened trading significantly higher and closed out the day at around $97. Despite shares falling to $85 on Friday afternoon amid a broader tech-fueled stock retreat , the company is still worth around $1.1 trillion—surpassing the market cap of Walmart .

The record IPO is great news for the cofounders and insiders who have been supporting Anthropic since it was founded in 2021. The biggest gains, though, belong to Amazon and Google, whose stakes are worth about $316 billion combined—more than twice the roughly $142 billion held by the seven cofounders. Here are some of the people and companies who stand to benefit the…

items.title: The Guardian view on Britain and Europe: Burnham’s reset cannot be the final destination | Editorial
items.summary:
It’s welcome news that Labour has reopened doors that the Conservatives slammed shut. But the fundamental dilemma over European integration remains

Andy Burnham on Friday announced a long-awaited deal to ease some of Brexit’s barriers. But EU sources say the agreements, or at least some of them, won’t take effect until Britain has resolved a dispute over its demand for European students to pay the same university tuition fees as British ones. The prime minister had hoped to turn the page on Brexit’s endless haggling. Instead, he was reminded that closer ties come at a price. This does not negate his achievement. The deals ease trade barriers on food, shield British exporters from EU carbon tariffs and let up to 100,000 young people on each side live and work across the Channel for three years. But Mr Burnham cannot claim an unqualified diplomatic victory.

Clearly, such an advance would have been unimaginable under the Conservatives or Reform. The Tories say they will rip up the agreements, though that stance carries the risk of alienating voters lost to the Liberal Democrats in 2024. Nigel Farage

items.title: Senate passes first-ever prediction market bill as Democrats turn up heat on upstart industry
items.summary:
Prediction markets are facing new limits on Capitol Hill. The Senate passed a bill Thursday evening that would bar platforms from offering contracts tied to terrorism, assassination, an individual’s death, war, or U.S. military operations—the first legislation targeting the burgeoning industry to clear either chamber of Congress.

Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and John Curtis (R-Utah) introduced the bill, formally called the DEATH BETS Act, to prevent exchanges and clearinghouses overseen by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission from offering or processing those contracts. It would also ban contracts whose outcomes are reasonably expected to depend mainly on someone’s death, even if the wording does not mention death. 

The bill passed the Senate by a voice vote and must still pass the House before heading to the president’s desk.

“They are offered with no regard for national security and in far too many cases, even basic morality,” Schiff said on the Senate floor. “These markets are operating in a Wild West, desperately in need of regulation and guardrails.”

As platforms like Kalshi and Polymarket have grown in prominence over the past two years, they have offered contracts on seemingly anything , drawing scrutiny over bets tied to war, violence, or human suffering. They have also raised concerns about insider trading, as users can trade without publicly revealing their identities, making it harder for outsiders to spot potential conflicts of interest.

Several cases have drawn politicians’ attention to these issues. One involved a Polymarket trader who made more than…

items.title: Fresh off a record $3 billion CMU pledge, Ken Griffin sends Pittsburgh 3 dinosaurs and $5 million
items.summary:
Nearly two months after his record-breaking $3 billion pledge to Carnegie Mellon University, billionaire Ken Griffin is sending Pittsburgh three dinosaurs.

The founder and CEO of Citadel is lending three rare long-necked dinosaur fossils to the Carnegie Museum of Natural History for 10 years, alongside a $5 million donation to support paleontological research and education, the museum announced Wednesday.

The deal adds to the tens of millions of dollars Griffin has already poured into dinosaur collecting, research, and exhibitions. It also keeps a rare find in scientists’ hands at a time when record auction prices are pushing more fossils into private collections, a trend many paleontologists warn could put specimens out of research’s reach.

The fossils, nicknamed Daisy, Lucky, and Lucy, belong to three plant-eating sauropods, one adult and two juveniles, discovered together in roughly 150-million-year-old rock in Wyoming and excavated between 2023 and 2025. Pittsburgh public radio station WESA reports that all three are Diplodocus carnegii , the same species as Dippy, the museum’s most famous dinosaur, which was named for founder Andrew Carnegie .

Griffin purchased the fossils last year through Sotheby’s for an undisclosed amount, according to the Financial Times .

Finding an adult and two young animals together gives researchers a rare chance to study how these dinosaurs grew and potentially interacted, according to a statement from Griffin Catalyst , Griffin’s philanthropic initiative. Scientists will also examine fossilized skin that the Pittsburgh Post-Gazette…
items.t: Fresh off a record $3 billion CMU pledge, Ken Griffin sends Pittsburgh 3 dinosaurs and $5 million

items.title: Someone did the math on the Democrats’ first-100-days agenda: It saves $30 billion on the Iran war but adds $4.1 trillion to the national debt
items.summary:
While it’s the responsibility of the U.S. Department of the Treasury to finance the interest on the $40 trillion national debt, it is members of both parties in Congress who have added to Uncle Sam’s borrowing.

With the Democrats winning a wave of seats in the midterm elections, everyone from Wall Street analysts to CEOs of America’s largest companies are wondering what a more divided government will mean.

Budget watchdogs are doing the same, and the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget (CRFB) has put a number on how much the Democrats’ plan for their first 100 days will cost.

The Democrats will go into the 120th Congress with slim majorities in both chambers, and they have been clear about what they want to achieve in their first three months with more power. Hakeem Jeffries, nominated by Democrats to serve as Speaker of the House, wrote in November that they aim to “reverse the Medicaid cuts, restore SNAP funding, extend the Affordable Care Act tax credits, eradicate the Trump tariffs, and stop the reckless war of choice in Iran.”

Some factors come with obvious budget implications: De-escalating the war in the Middle East would save money, while ending Trump tariffs would axe a revenue stream that generated $287 billion in customs duties, taxes, and fees in 2025 per the Richmond Fed—up 192% on the prior year. 

The CRFB estimates that, in total, the “first 100 days” policies would cost $4.1 trillion through 2037. Without offsets (spending cuts or revenue increases used to balance new policies), $4.9 trillion would be added to the debt burden over the next…
items.t: Someone did the math on the Democrats’ first-100-days agenda: It saves $30 billion on the Iran war but adds $4.1 trillion to the national debt

items.title: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers
items.summary:
It’s time to rethink welfare as AI reshapes the economy and wears down the brains of some of the most vulnerable workers

AI is adding to the cognitive load of workers already stretched thin by unpredictable pay, insecure housing and mounting debt – and the lowest paid feel it most. We need to rethink welfare for an economy being reshaped by AI.

Throughout the history of the study of economics, the human brain, which directs our labour, judgment and resilience, has rarely been considered an asset in its own right. The emerging AI economy is changing that. As machines take on routine work, what becomes most valuable is the judgment, creativity and insights only people can provide. Economists coined a term for this in recent years: brain capital.

Professor Dame Henrietta Moore is founder and director of the UCL Institute for Global Prosperity and co-leads The New Alignment, the institute’s G20 policy programme

Continue reading...
items.t: AI is imposing a hidden ‘cognitive tax’ on the lowest-paid workers

items.title: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier
items.summary:
Our tech infrastructure is riddled with problems. But they’re all downstream of the incentives baked into shareholder capitalism

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at Microsoft, the FAA, a handful of banks, United Airlines, an unnamed classified NSA network, and Apple. People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyber-attack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyber-attack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

items.t: Don’t blame cyber-attacks for recent outages. The real villain is the US economy | Bruce Schneier

In the end, Anthropic’s much-anticipated IPO more than lived up to the hype. The market’s embrace of one of the AI industry’s most talked about companies has resulted in the maker of the Claude chatbot becoming one of the world’s most valuable firms after just one day of trading.

With many of the company’s founders, investors and employees now worth billions of dollars – and demand for the company’s stock remaining resilient – attention now turns to the stability of the wider market, and the global headwinds that experts say could threaten the AI industry over the coming months.

items.title: Anthropic keeps the AI party swinging, but the atmosphere is bubbly | Nils Pratley
items.summary:
Can the newly listed AI company really be worth $2tn? Anyone who remembers the late 1990s has good reason to ask

Roll up, roll up, who wants to buy shares in a company whose technology “could pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”, as the prospectus had it? Virtually everybody, as it turned out. Anthropic flew out of the blocks on its first day as a listed company.

From the point of view of the promoters, the result was as good as it gets. The final pricing for the shares at $83 apiece was meaningfully higher than the indicated range of $70 to $78, but still left room for a big initial “pop”. There were positive vibes all round – especially for the battalion of investment banks collecting $550m of underwriting fees.

items.title: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale
items.summary:
Julia Garner and Anthony Boyle play the FTX founders behind ‘the greatest fraud ever committed’ in the US. It’s a mind-boggling story – just make sure you don’t miss a single moment

What happens when you put really stupid clever people in charge of the world? Not as presidents (they currently trend mostly towards the merely stupid) or prime ministers (generally neither really stupid nor really clever), but in charge of the real world, which is to say the online world, the one that really governs us? We are watching that play out day by day, but if you have enough slack left in your dread-system, a cortisol spike yet to execute, why not add a warning from history to your consumption of horrors?

Welcome to The Altruists, a breakneck breakdown of the brief career of Sam Bankman-Fried (played by Anthony Boyle) who, with his on-off girlfriend Caroline Ellison (played by Julia Garner), set up the cryptocurrency exchange FTX with the belief that it would revolutionise finance and – as the increasingly absurd/dishonest/knowingly satirical Silicon Valley mantra has it – make the world a better place. A very few years later, FTX – worth $36bn (£27bn) at its peak – collapsed and in 2023 the pair were convicted of various charges deriving from what the trial judge called “the greatest financial fraud ever perpetrated in this country”. Ellison was sentenced to two years in prison after testifying against Bankman-Fried. Bankman-Fried is serving 25 years and was ordered to forfeit $11bn (£8.3bn). He says he is innocent and is applying to the supreme court to review his…
items.t: The Altruists review – two of TV’s best actors light up this chaotic crypto tale
